readerTitle: Same discount, different deal: how you give ground matters
caseNote: 가상 사례 (운송 회사 두 곳, 소프트웨어 갱신 협상) + 실제 연구 (Cialdini 외 1975, 양보의 상호성)
insight: 양보는 돈이 아니라 메시지다. 얼마를 깎았는지보다 어떤 순서와 조건으로 깎았는지가 상대에게 내 한계를 알려준다.
misconception: 협상은 결국 얼마나 깎아 주느냐의 문제다. 같은 금액을 양보하면 결과도 같다.

sources.text: Cialdini, R. B., Vincent, J. E., Lewis, S. K., Catalan, J., Wheeler, D., & Darby, B. L. (1975). Reciprocal concessions procedure for inducing compliance: The door-in-the-face technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 31(2), 206–215.
운송 회사와 소프트웨어 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Cialdini 외(1975) 수치 확인 필요: 직접 요청 시 약 17%(16.7%) 동의, 큰 요청(2년간 주 2시간 봉사) 거절 후 동물원 동행 2시간 요청 시 약 50% 동의. 원문 실험 1의 수치와 대상(대학생, 청소년 비행 상담 프로그램)을 게시 전 확인하세요.
소프트웨어 사례: 200석 × 월 $30 = 월 $6,000, 연 $72,000. 20% 할인 시 연 $14,400 감소, 12% 한도는 연 $8,640 감소. 카드에는 비율만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Same discount, different deal: how you give ground matters
body: Two trucking companies bid on the same $120,000 contract with a food manufacturer. Over four rounds of talks, each cut its price by exactly $12,000.
One signed that week. The other was still being squeezed a month later. The difference was not how much they gave. It was how they gave it.

image.label: Two delivery trucks facing the same warehouse
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 식품 공장 창고 앞에 트럭 두 대가 나란히 서 있음. 한 트럭 옆에는 악수하는 두 손, 다른 트럭 옆에는 계속 쌓여 가는 서류 더미. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The buyer wants 10% off.
body: You run a trucking firm. A food manufacturer likes your $120,000 bid for a year of deliveries. Then its buyer says: "Take 10% off and we'll sign today."

options.text: Meet halfway: offer 5% off right away
options.feedback: It feels fair and keeps things moving. But you gave $6,000 for nothing, and the buyer now knows a single push is worth 5%.

options.text: Offer 3% off if they sign a two-year contract
options.feedback: A smaller step, tied to something you value. The buyer learns that each move costs them something too.
You protect your margin, but zero movement can read as bad faith. The buyer may walk to a rival who looks more flexible.

cards.title: Same total, different message.
body: Steady Freight cut $3,000 every round. North Haul cut $6,000, then $3,500, then $1,800, then $700.
Steady's buyer saw a pattern: every push is worth $3,000. So she pushed again. North Haul's buyer watched the steps shrink toward zero and concluded he had found the floor.

cards.title: Making concessions
body: **Making concessions** well means giving ground in a way that tells the other side where your limit is, and gets something back each time.

Every concession carries two things: value and information. The size of each step, how fast it comes and what you ask in return all tell the other side how much room is left. They will negotiate against that message, not against your spreadsheet.

image.label: Staircase of shrinking steps leading to a floor
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽은 높이가 똑같은 계단(끝없이 이어지는 점선), 오른쪽은 점점 낮아지는 계단이 바닥선에 닿음. 오른쪽 바닥선에 "Your limit" 라벨. 색은 차분하게, 오른쪽 계단만 강조색.

cards.title: Giving ground invites giving ground.
body: In a 1975 study, Robert Cialdini and colleagues asked students to chaperone young offenders on a two-hour zoo trip. Asked directly, about 17% agreed.
Other students were first asked for a much bigger commitment: two hours a week for two years. After they refused, the researchers retreated to the zoo trip. About **50%** agreed.
The retreat felt like a concession, and people answered with one of their own. A step back can pull the other side forward, as long as they see it as a real step.

cards.title: Three habits that make a concession count.
body: These turn a concession into a signal you control.
list: **Shrink the steps:** large to small says you're nearing your limit. Equal steps say more is coming.
**Trade, don't give:** phrase it as "If you…, then I…". A longer contract, faster payment, a bigger order.
**Name the cost:** say what the step takes from you. A step that looks free gets treated as free.
cards.callout: Unconditional concessions teach the other side that pushing pays.

cards.title: Don't fake your room.
body: Shrinking steps only work if they're honest. If you pad your first price just to have something to give away, experienced buyers learn to discount everything you say, and they remember it next year.

Speed matters in both directions. Never moving can look like bad faith, even when your price is fair. Saying yes too fast backfires too: the other side may wonder if they asked for too little and feel worse about a good deal.

cards.title: Now it's a software renewal.
body: You sell scheduling software to a clinic chain: 200 seats at $30 per seat a month. At renewal, their operations lead says a rival is cheaper and asks for 20% off.
You can go to 12% at most. What do you offer?

options.text: Give 20% right away so they don't churn
options.feedback: You keep the account, but you blow past your limit and teach them that every renewal starts with a threat.

options.text: Offer 8% for annual prepay, up to 12% for a two-year term, and say that's the floor
options.feedback: Each step is smaller and buys you something: cash up front, then a longer commitment. Naming the floor makes the last step believable.

options.text: Offer 12% straight away and call it your best price
options.feedback: Honest and quick, but you spent all your room in one move and got nothing back. With no shrinking steps, "best price" is harder to believe.

cards.title: Every concession says something. Make it say "nearly done."
body: Give in shrinking steps, ask for something each time, and name what each step costs you.
**Try it today:** before your next negotiation, write down your opening, your limit and three planned steps between them. Make each smaller than the last, and pair each with something you'll ask for.
